title: ℚ Satisfies All CDLO Axioms
content: These six instance declarations assemble the typeclass evidence that ℚ is a Countable Dense Linear Order Without endpoints (CDLO). Each instance delegates to Mathlib's existing typeclass infrastructure for ℚ. Together they form the precondition package required by Cantor's characterization theorem.
mathContext: A CDLO is a structure $(X, <)$ satisfying: (1) $X$ is countable, (2) $<$ is a linear (total) order, (3) density: $\forall a < b,\, \exists c: a < c < b$, (4) no minimum: $\forall x,\, \exists y < x$, (5) no maximum: $\forall x,\, \exists y > x$, (6) non-empty. All six hold for $\mathbb{Q}$.

title: Spelling Out Density and No-Endpoints
content: Three theorems make the abstract CDLO axioms concrete for ℚ: density (`rationals_dense`), no minimum (`rationals_no_min`), and no maximum (`rationals_no_max`). Each is a one-line consequence of the corresponding typeclass. Spelling these out serves a pedagogical role: they demonstrate that the abstract axioms have explicit, constructive witnesses.
mathContext: Density: $\forall p < q \in \mathbb{Q},\, \exists r \in \mathbb{Q}: p < r < q$. No min: $\forall q \in \mathbb{Q},\, \exists p \in \mathbb{Q}: p < q$. No max: $\forall q \in \mathbb{Q},\, \exists r \in \mathbb{Q}: q < r$.

title: Cantor's Characterization Theorem
content: The central result: any countable dense linear order without endpoints is order-isomorphic to ℚ. The proof is a single delegation to Mathlib's `Order.iso_of_countable_dense`, which encapsulates the full back-and-forth construction. This theorem shows that ℚ is not just an example of a CDLO — it is the canonical representative, uniquely determined up to isomorphism by its order-theoretic properties alone.
mathContext: If $(\alpha, <)$ is a CDLO, then $\alpha \cong_{\mathrm{ord}} \mathbb{Q}$, i.e., there exists an order-isomorphism $f: \alpha \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb{Q}$. In first-order logic: $\mathbb{Q}$ is the unique countable model (up to isomorphism) of the theory DLO (Dense Linear Orders without endpoints).

title: Uniqueness: Any Two CDLOs Are Isomorphic
content: A direct corollary of the characterization: since both orders are isomorphic to ℚ, they are isomorphic to each other. This is stated as an independent theorem (`countable_dense_linear_orders_iso`) with full generality — two arbitrary types α and β satisfying the CDLO axioms. The proof is again a single application of `Order.iso_of_countable_dense`.
mathContext: If $(\alpha, <_\alpha)$ and $(\beta, <_\beta)$ are both CDLOs, then $\alpha \cong_{\mathrm{ord}} \beta$. Proof: $\alpha \cong \mathbb{Q} \cong \beta$, so by transitivity $\alpha \cong \beta$. In model theory, this is ω-categoricity of DLO.

title: Back-and-Forth Infrastructure: PartialIso
content: This section exposes Mathlib's `Order.PartialIso` type — the building block of the back-and-forth construction. A `PartialIso α β` is a finite partial order-isomorphism (a finite set of pairs). The `.comm` operation swaps domain and codomain, used in the back-step of the construction. The `density_extension_lemma` formalizes the key combinatorial fact: given finite lower bounds `lo` and upper bounds `hi` with `lo < hi`, some element exists strictly between all of them.
mathContext: A partial isomorphism $f: A \hookrightarrow B$ (finite) can be extended: given a new element $a \in \alpha \setminus \mathrm{dom}(f)$, density guarantees $\exists b \in \beta$ with $f(a') < b < f(a'')$ for all $a' < a < a''$ in $\mathrm{dom}(f)$. The lemma `Order.exists_between_finsets` formalizes this for finite sets.

title: Self-Similarity of ℚ
content: ℚ is isomorphic to itself as an ordered set — but not only via the identity. The theorem `rationals_selfsimilar` uses the back-and-forth method to produce a *non-trivial* automorphism. This reflects ℚ's extreme homogeneity: the automorphism group of ℚ acts transitively on all finite configurations, making ℚ homogeneous as a model.
mathContext: The automorphism group $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{Q}, <)$ is large: it acts oligomorphically (finitely many orbits on $n$-tuples for each $n$). In particular, for any two $n$-tuples $\bar{a}, \bar{b} \in \mathbb{Q}^n$ with the same order type, there exists $\sigma \in \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{Q}, <)$ with $\sigma(\bar{a}) = \bar{b}$.

title: Embedding ℤ and ℕ into ℚ
content: Two order embeddings are constructed explicitly: `integers_embed : ℤ ↪o ℚ` (the canonical inclusion $n \mapsto n$) and `naturals_embed : ℕ ↪o ℚ`. Both use the `OrderEmbedding` structure with explicit proofs of injectivity (`inj'`) and order-preservation (`map_rel_iff'`). These complement the isomorphism results: ℚ not only characterizes countable dense linear orders but also contains all countable well-orders as substructures.
mathContext: An order embedding $f: \alpha \hookrightarrow \beta$ satisfies $a \leq b \iff f(a) \leq f(b)$. The canonical embedding $\mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Q}$ sends $n \mapsto n/1$. Key facts used: `Int.cast_injective` (injectivity of $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Q}$) and `Int.cast_le` (order preservation).

title: Concrete Density Witnesses
content: Three concrete results demonstrate density explicitly: the midpoint formula, an explicit numeric example (5/12 lies between 1/3 and 1/2), and halving a positive rational. The midpoint theorem uses `linarith` — the linear arithmetic decision procedure. These serve as verification examples and make the abstract density axiom tangible.
mathContext: The midpoint $m = (p+q)/2$ satisfies $p < m < q$ when $p < q$, since $p < (p+q)/2 \iff 2p < p+q \iff p < q$. Linear arithmetic over $\mathbb{Q}$ is decidable (it is a quantifier-free fragment of the reals).

title: Constructive No-Endpoint Witnesses
content: Two one-liners provide explicit witnesses for no-minimum and no-maximum: the predecessor `q - 1 < q` and successor `q < q + 1`. These are immediate from `linarith` and formalize the obvious arithmetic fact that shifting by ±1 moves strictly up or down.
mathContext: For any $q \in \mathbb{Q}$: $q - 1 < q$ and $q < q + 1$. These witnesses show $\mathbb{Q}$ has no endpoints, complementing `NoMinOrder` and `NoMaxOrder` instances with concrete arithmetic witnesses.

title: Infinite Density: Two and Three Points Between Any Gap
content: By iterated application of density, we can find two (`two_between`) and three (`three_between`) distinct rationals strictly between any two. More generally, density can be iterated to find arbitrarily many points between any two — a reflection of the fact that ℚ has no 'atoms' in its order structure. This foreshadows that every open interval in ℚ contains infinitely many (in fact, countably many) rationals.
mathContext: By induction, for any $n$ and $p < q$ in $\mathbb{Q}$, there exist $r_1 < r_2 < \cdots < r_n$ all in $(p, q)$. Proof: apply density $n-1$ times. Each application uses: if $a < b$ then $\exists c: a < c < b$.

title: Cardinal Arithmetic: |ℚ| = ℵ₀
content: Two cardinal results connect the order-theoretic results to set theory: the cardinality of ℚ is ℵ₀ (aleph-null, the smallest infinite cardinal), and ℚ and ℕ have the same cardinality. These formalize the countability of ℚ in the language of cardinal arithmetic. The proof uses `Cardinal.mk_denumerable`, which states that the cardinality of any `Denumerable` type is ℵ₀.
mathContext: $|\mathbb{Q}| = \aleph_0 = |\mathbb{N}|$. This follows from the Schröder-Bernstein theorem: $\mathbb{N} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable, so $|\mathbb{Q}| = \aleph_0$. In Lean, `Denumerable ℚ` witnesses the bijection $\mathbb{Q} \cong \mathbb{N}$.

title: ℤ Is Discrete: No Integer Lies Strictly Between n and n+1
content: A stark contrast to ℚ: the integers have no density. `no_integer_between` proves there is no integer strictly between n and n+1, using the `omega` tactic (a decision procedure for linear integer arithmetic). This highlights the qualitative difference between ℤ (discrete order) and ℚ (dense order), even though both are countable.
mathContext: The integers $\mathbb{Z}$ form a *discrete* linear order: every element $n$ has an immediate successor $n+1$ with no element strictly between them. Formally: $\neg \exists m \in \mathbb{Z}: n < m < n+1$. The `omega` tactic decides this via Presburger arithmetic.

title: Universality: Every Finite Order Embeds into ℚ
content: The universality theorem `fin_embeds` establishes that any finite linear order Fin n embeds strictly monotonically into ℚ. Combined with `integers_embed`, this shows ℚ is universal for all countable linear orders. The map $k \mapsto k$ (casting Fin n to ℕ to ℚ) is the canonical witness. This is the finite case of the broader theorem that every countable linear order embeds into ℚ.
mathContext: Universality of $\mathbb{Q}$: every countable linear order $(L, <)$ admits an order-preserving injection $L \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Q}$. For finite orders $\mathrm{Fin}\, n = \{0, 1, \ldots, n-1\}$, the map $k \mapsto k$ (cast to $\mathbb{Q}$) works since $\mathbb{N} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Q}$ is order-preserving.

title: Verification Examples
content: Three inline `example` declarations serve as end-to-end verification: the characterization applied to ℚ itself produces an automorphism, the midpoint formula works on 1/4 and 3/4, and the embedding `integers_embed` respects order (3 < 5). These examples are type-checked by Lean and serve as smoke tests that all pieces fit together.
mathContext: The example `integers_embed 3 < integers_embed 5` reduces to showing $(3 : \mathbb{Q}) < 5$, proved by `norm_num`. The midpoint example verifies $(1/4 + 3/4)/2 = 1/2$ satisfies $1/4 < 1/2 < 3/4$, again by `norm_num`.
